newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF now set to negotiate on help for Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: IMF now set to negotiate on help for Bulgaria.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) will resume talks on crucial aid to pull Bulgaria back from the brink of debt default as soon as an interim government is in place, an IMF official said on Wednesday.
The IMF welcomed Bulgaria's decision to hold early national elections by April 20 as the ex-communist ruling party bowed to opposition pressure on Tuesday.
The Balkan country, with its economy sliding into chaos for months, had been paralyzed by widespread strikes and 30 days of mass demonstrations to force elections two years early.
The IMF, which has delayed vital funding, and the European Union have said no help would be forthcoming until the political crisis was sorted out.
"The IMF mission is prepared to come immediately after the interim government is appointed," an IMF official who declined to be named told Reuters.
President Petar Stoyanov must appoint an interim cabinet by February 20 whose main role will be to organise the elections.
This cabinet could also prepare, jointly with the IMF, measures for implementation of a strict monetary mechanism by the next parliament and government.
"Bulgarian political forces would be expected to guarantee a commitment to the programme by both the interim government and the government which will be in power after elections," said the official.
The IMF proposed the implementation of a currency board last year to halt the free fall of the national currency, the lev, and to restore confidence in ailing local banks.
The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing financial powers of the government and the central bank.
"Bulgaria's economy has become a moving target now and stricter measures will be needed to contain the crisis. The currency board alone will not be enough," said the official.
The currency board system must be accompanied by radical structural reform, including closing loss-making enterprises and banks.
Bulgaria's shattered economy went into a nosedive while politicians squabbled for the past month on how to resolve the deadlock.

With January inflation expected at more than 50 percent, hyperinflation has become a factor for the first time. Long queues of consumers have formed outside bread shops to stockpile food before prices go up the next day.
The lev collapsed to 3,000 per dollar on Wednesday from 600 in the beginning of the year and the central bank has exhausted its arsenal of monetary instruments to support the lev.
Foreign exchange reserves fell $415 million in January and there is a shortage of cash for vital imports such as fuel and grain.
Imposing a temporary freeze of personal savings in banks is another measure being considered, said the official.
It would include replacing personal deposits with government securities which would be redeemed later on maturity dates.
